common_name: Zeylanicum Crinum Lily (Red-Striped Milk-and-Wine Lily Species)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to light shade; this is the true wild species behind the 'milk-and-wine lily' common name, distinct from the more cold-hardy Gulf South hybrid Crinum x herbertii. Native across tropical Africa and Asia, it is less frost-tolerant than the Southern pass-along hybrids and appreciates a sheltered site or mulch outside zone 9b. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in rich, well-drained to consistently moist soil in full sun to light shade, and expect the plant to resent being disturbed once established. The signature trait is the flower itself: each of the six petals is white to pale pink with a broad, dark red to crimson median stripe running its length, giving the umbels of 6-12 funnel-shaped blooms a distinctive candy-striped look repeated through the warm season rather than in a single flush. Strap-shaped leaves reach 2-3 feet and are evergreen where winters stay mild. Because this species carries less cold tolerance than the C. bulbispermum-derived hybrids more commonly grown in Southern gardens, site it in a warm, sheltered spot and mulch heavily if grown near the northern edge of its range.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cape Coast lily is a widespread, deciduous South African species found from the Eastern Cape north into tropical Africa, and like its relative C. bulbispermum it is deciduous and notably cold-hardy for the genus, tolerating winter dormancy with the foliage dying back completely. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Plant the large bulb with its neck at soil level in well-drained garden soil in full sun, where it will go fully dormant and lose its leaves each winter before re-emerging in spring. Umbels of 6-12 fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers appear in late spring to early summer, usually just ahead of or alongside the new leaves, in shades from white to pink with a deeper rose stripe down each petal. Its wide native range across summer-rainfall regions of southern and eastern Africa has made it an important, tough parent behind many cold-hardy garden crinum hybrids, and it tolerates both seasonal drought during dormancy and heavier soils better than more tropical species. Leave large clumps undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the bulb matures and offsets.

common_name: Mrs. James Hendry Crinum (Classic Soft-Pink Southern Pass-Along Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a durable old Southern heirloom cultivar passed down through gardens for generations, prized for vigor and reliable bloom rather than novelty. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck near the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and then leave the clump largely alone, since this heirloom cultivar performs best once it has settled in and multiplied. Large, soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers open in umbels atop stout scapes in summer, with a fragrance that carries well in the evening garden. Like many of the old Southern pass-along crinums, it is exceptionally tough, tolerating heat, humidity, heavy clay, and periods of drought once established, and it has been handed down between Gulf South gardeners for decades under this name well before more recent trademarked introductions arrived on the market. Divide only when clumps become overcrowded, as flowering typically improves for several years after undisturbed establishment.
sources: Scott Ogden, Garden Bulbs for the South

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to light shade; native to the coastal thickets of Tanzania, Zanzibar, and neighboring East Africa, it is evergreen and less cold-hardy than the South African crinums, best suited to warm zone 9b-11 gardens or containers brought under cover in colder areas. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and keep evenly moist through the growing season since this coastal East African species does not experience the pronounced dry dormancy of some of its relatives. Fragrant white flowers, each petal marked with a fine maroon to reddish-brown stripe on the reverse, open in umbels through the warm months and are most noticeably scented after dusk. The strap-shaped, glossy leaves stay evergreen in frost-free conditions, so gardeners outside the warmest zones do best growing it in a large container that can be moved to shelter in winter. Established clumps are otherwise low-maintenance and resent frequent division, flowering more heavily as bulbs mature.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
